idiom_name: test-only subclass overriding the self-call boundary
implementation_notes: Test-only subclass of the System Under Test: move (or find) the call that reaches the unusable dependency in its own small, overridable method - Meszaros's Self-Call - and override exactly that method in a subclass that lives with the tests, giving it a canned value, an empty body or a recording body. When the dependency is fetched through an accessor or a singleton lookup rather than constructed inline, override the accessor so it returns the prepared double; when the test needs to initialize or observe internals, add state setters and getters (or extra exposing methods) to the same subclass, which is what turns it into a control/observation point. Relax the seam's visibility no further than protected, instantiate the subclass in the fixture's creation method instead of the production class, and keep the subclass out of the production build - that is what distinguishes the pattern from shipping test logic in production.
code_sketch:
class TimeDisplay                 # SUT: hard-codes the boundary it uses
    getTime()  { return realClock.now() }   # the seam (small, single-purpose)
    formatHtml() { return render(getTime()) }   # self-call reaches the seam

class TimeDisplayTss extends TimeDisplay    # test-only subclass
    override getTime() { return FIXED }     # control point: canned boundary
    setTime(t) { FIXED = t }                # extra method: test-only configuration

sut = new TimeDisplayTss(); sut.setTime(midnight)
assert sut.formatHtml() == midnightHtml
pitfalls: Overriding the method that contains the behaviour under test: the fixture then replaces the logic it claims to verify, and the test can pass for the wrong reason.
The seam only exists if the boundary call is its own overridable method with visible access; a boundary buried in a long method or behind a private/final member needs production to be edited first.
Substituted singletons and statics are global state: without deterministic teardown the double leaks into unrelated tests.

The double runs the real superclass constructor: a plain test-specific subclass inherits every constructor side effect (opened connections, singleton registrations, file handles); generated-subclass tools can skip the base constructor (PHPUnit disableOriginalConstructor) but a hand-written subclass executes it - construct the fixture where those effects are harmless or extract them first.

Configuring the double can itself execute the real boundary: when(spy.fetch()).thenReturn(canned) calls the real fetch() first, so stub spies with doReturn(...).when(spy).fetch() and NSubstitute void members with When(...).DoNotCallBase() - otherwise the setup triggers the very side effect the override was meant to prevent.
